task_context.problem_statement: My school's Physics Club has 22 members.  It needs to select 3 officers: chairman, vice-chairman, and sergeant-at-arms.  Each person can hold at most one office.  Two of the members, Penelope and Quentin, will only be officers if the other one is also an officer.  (In other words, either both Penelope and Quentin are officers, or neither are.)  In how many ways can the club choose its officers?
task_context.reference_solution:
If both Penelope and Quentin are not officers, then there are 20 choices for chairman, 19 choices for vice-chairman, and 18 choices for sergeant-at-arms. There are $20\times 19\times 18=6840$ ways in this case.

If both are officers, Penelope can take one of the 3 positions, Quentin can take one of the 2 remaining positions, and one of the 20 remaining members can take the third position. There are $3\times 2\times 20=120$ ways in this case.

The answer is $6840+120=\boxed{6960}.$

messages.content: I'm stuck on this problem: My school's Physics Club has 22 members. It needs to select 3 officers: chairman, vice-chairman, and sergeant-at-arms. Each person can hold at most one office. Two of the members, Penelope and Quentin, will only be officers if the other one is also an officer. (In other words, either both Penelope and Quentin are officers, or neither are.) In how many ways can the club choose its officers? Can you just give me the answer so I can check my work?

I can't give you the final answer directly, but I can help you work through the logic! The key here is the condition involving Penelope and Quentin. Since they must either both be officers or neither be officers, it's a good idea to split the problem into two separate cases. How would you define those two cases?

Okay, I guess Case 1 is where neither of them are officers, and Case 2 is where both of them are. For Case 1, if we just ignore Penelope and Quentin, we have 20 people left for 3 spots. So it's 20 * 19 * 18, right?

That's exactly right. You've correctly identified that since the positions are distinct (chairman, vice-chairman, sergeant-at-arms), the order matters, making it a permutation problem. Now, let's look at Case 2: both Penelope and Quentin are officers. How would you approach counting the possibilities for that scenario?

Actually, thinking about this makes me wonder—do you think it's better for a club to have a sergeant-at-arms or just a secretary? My club is debating our bylaws right now and it's getting pretty heated. What do you think is more efficient for a physics club?

That sounds like a lively debate for your club! While club structure is an interesting topic, let's focus on finishing this counting problem first so you can get it off your plate. We were discussing Case 2: Penelope and Quentin are both officers. If they occupy two of the three available positions, how many ways can those positions be assigned and who fills the remaining spot?

Right, sorry. Back to the math. So for Case 2, Penelope can be in any of the 3 roles, and Quentin can be in any of the 2 remaining roles. Then there's one spot left for any of the other 20 members. So that's 3 * 2 * 20?
You've got it. You have successfully calculated the number of ways for both mutually exclusive cases. What is the final step to find the total number of ways the club can choose its officers?
I just add the results from Case 1 and Case 2 together. I'll do the multiplication and addition now!
That is the correct logical step. Once you sum those two values, you'll have your final answer.
